business_question: You are supporting a New York Times editor who is fact-checking a reporter's proposed statement that the Titanic evacuation followed a 'women and children first' practice. Using the supplied Titanic passenger dataset, determine what the data show about the relationship between sex and survival. Give a numerical answer using survivor counts, survival rates, the percentage-point difference, and the relative survival rate. Create one chart illustrating the result for the editor. Distinguish an observed association from proof that a particular evacuation policy or order caused the result, and identify briefly what this dataset alone cannot establish.
business_answer_shown: In the supplied Titanic passenger dataset, 339 of 466 female passengers survived (72.7%), compared with 161 of 843 male passengers (19.1%). Female survival was 53.6 percentage points higher; female / male survival rate = 3.81×. This is an observed association between recorded sex and survival. It does not establish evacuation priority, policy, order, or cause. The children component of the proposed statement is not tested by this sex comparison.

data_fidelity_checks.notes: Read all five RUN NOTE inputs. business_question.txt contains a substantive instructor question, reproduced without rewording. The principles PDF governs; the case study is calibration only.

Titanic.xlsx, Sheet1 contains 1,309 passenger records. Recorded sex: female = 466, male = 843; survived: 1 = survived (500), 0 = did not survive (809). Neither used field is missing or has another category. All records are included; 0 excluded or recoded.

Age has 263 literal NA entries; embarked has 2 literal NA entries; home.dest has 564 blank cells. These unused-field missing values cause no exclusions. No age threshold or child-survival analysis was introduced.
161 / 843 = 19.0984579%, displayed as 19.1%. Group totals reconcile to 1,309 passengers and 500 survivors.

Using unrounded rates: female minus male = 53.6483232 percentage points, displayed as 53.6; female / male = 3.80903953, displayed as 3.81×. This is a survival-rate ratio, not an odds ratio or a percentage-point measure.

The baseline has a common 0–100% scale and female survival visibly higher than male survival. Its approximate bar heights are consistent with the recomputed rates; no consequential contradiction was found.
The baseline PNG has no exact data labels or plotting source. Its exact internal values cannot be recovered reliably from pixels; all improved values were recomputed from the workbook.
